clue.text: But G.B.S. beaten up here by Dolly ?

indicators.note: beating something up, like eggs or washing, mixes it about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: G.B.S. is George Bernard Shaw, the playwright, known by his initials

explanation.surface: Someone complains that the playwright Shaw was thrashed by a woman called Dolly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beaten up' shuffles BUT with SHAW. A dolly was a wooden paddle for pounding clothes in a laundry tub, so 'here by Dolly' is the place where the washing gets beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: A dolly is an old laundry tool used to pound clothes, and the vessel it works in is a wooden tub of soapy water.

clue.text: Candidate for the Order of Merit ?

definitions.text: Candidate for the Order of Merit

parts.words: Candidate for the Order of Merit
parts.note: the Order of Merit is a British honour for great distinction, so a candidate must be deserving

explanation.surface: Someone being considered for a British royal honour.
explanation.walkthrough: The Order of Merit is an exclusive British honour given by the monarch; anyone with merit is deserving.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of merit is deserving and estimable, the kind of notable fit for a high honour.

clue.text: Race with half the trouble to face

definitions.note: the definition is a noun, the answer an adjective naming a group of peoples

parts.note: semi- is the prefix for half
a tic is a twitch, a trouble that affects the face

explanation.surface: A race run with half the difficulty ahead of the runners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' looks like a contest, but it is the definition, a family of peoples; 'with' links.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective names the language family and peoples including Arabs and Jews, once called a race.

clue.text: Congreve's superstitious lord?

parts.note: Lord ... is a character in Congreve's play The Double Dealer, and his name is what the superstitious say to avert bad luck

explanation.surface: A question about a nobleman in a play who fears bad luck.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord Touchwood is in Congreve's comedy The Double Dealer; his name is also the charm said, while touching wood, to ward off bad luck.
explanation.definitionFit: People touch a wooden object and say this phrase to avert ill luck, and Congreve gave it to a peer.

clue.text: They aren't all Shylocks

parts.note: Shylock in The Merchant of Venice holds Antonio's bond, so the clue points to people who hold bonds

explanation.surface: A defence of a group unfairly called moneylenders.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock in Shakespeare's The Merchant of Venice demands his bond; investors who own bonds also hold bonds, but are not all so ruthless.
explanation.definitionFit: Investors owning government or company debt certificates hold bonds, as Shylock held his.

clue.text: The man an old B.E.F. corporal ? Sounds the same but isn't

parts.note: homo is Latin for man, as in Homo sapiens
Corporal Nym is a soldier in Shakespeare's Henry V, part of an English expeditionary force to France long before the B.E.F. (British Expeditionary Force) of the World Wars

explanation.surface: A question about some old soldier of the British Expeditionary Force, followed by a remark about sound.
explanation.walkthrough: The B.E.F. was Britain's army in France in both World Wars; Henry V's army was an earlier one, so Shakespeare's Corporal Nym counts as an old B.E.F. corporal.
explanation.definitionFit: Words alike in sound or spelling but different in meaning, like bear and bare, are given this grammatical label.

clue.text: This man accompanied Melville

parts.note: Melville's first name splits into this word followed by man, so this, with man accompanying it, comes before Melville

explanation.surface: A question about the companion of a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Herman Melville wrote Moby-Dick: 'This' plus 'man' gives his first name, so 'This man accompanied Melville' says the answer, with MAN after it, goes before his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Moby-Dick was named Herman, which is this pronoun with man added.

clue.text: I.andor's charming soother ?

parts.note: the poet Walter Savage Landor's middle name recalls 'charms to soothe a savage breast', what Congreve said of harmony

explanation.surface: A question about a poet's calming companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Congreve wrote that it 'has charms to soothe a savage breast'; the poet Walter Savage Landor had Savage as his middle name, so he is the savage being soothed.
explanation.definitionFit: Congreve's line says melody has charms to soothe a savage breast, and Landor's middle name was Savage.

clue.text: Nearly a dead-heat she assumes at last

parts.note: nigh is an old word for nearly
a race ending in a dead heat is a tie

explanation.surface: A race finishing almost level, which she takes on at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'she assumes at last' reads like a race report; it means what a woman puts on at the end of the day.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's loose sleeping gown is put on last thing at night.

clue.text: Time of high winds and a rough sea, noble lady

parts.note: March is the month known for gales

indicators.note: a rough sea is churned up, so its letters are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A noblewoman sails in a windy month on a heavy sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' shuffles SEA into ESA.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian marchioness, the wife or widow of a marquis, holds this title.

clue.text: Strange bean, of an undutiful spirit ?

definitions.note: the definition describes a person who deals in spirit on which no duty has been paid

parts.note: rum is old British slang for odd or strange
the runner is a kind of climbing bean

explanation.surface: An odd bean is described as having a disobedient character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undutiful spirit' sounds like a rebellious nature, but it means liquor smuggled without paying duty, the trade of a Prohibition-era smuggler.
explanation.definitionFit: A smuggler of liquor brings in spirits without paying customs duty, so his stock is undutiful spirit.

clue.text: Tease us in return, sweetie

indicators.note: in return means the whole run of letters from tease and us is read backwards

parts.note: to rag someone is to tease them

explanation.surface: A flirt asks to be teased back, calling the other person sweetie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in return' turns RAGUS round to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are terms of endearment for a loved one, like honey or darling.

clue.text: The way eggs get broken

parts.note: the clue reads like cookery, but it describes chicks breaking out of their shells, and the answer is also a doorway on a ship

explanation.surface: A cookery instruction on how to crack eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests cracking eggs into a pan; the answer is how chicks break out of eggs, and is also a way through a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicks emerge by cracking their shells from inside, a process also used as a verb for eggs opening.

clue.text: Jumpy Jacobites ? But game

parts.note: to hop is to jump, so jumpy is read as hopping
the Jacobite risings were largely Scottish, so Jacobites stands for the Scotch

explanation.surface: A remark that the Jacobite rebels were nervous, but plucky all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' reads as brave, but it is the definition, a children's playground game; 'But' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Children chalk squares on the ground and hop through them in this playground pastime.

clue.text: Tommy's comrade in arms in a division ?

definitions.text: Tommy's comrade in arms in a division

parts.words: Tommy's comrade in arms in a division
parts.note: a Tommy is a British soldier, whose fellow soldier might be ..., and a parliamentary division votes on a measure

explanation.surface: A British soldier's mate in an army division.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy is slang for a British soldier; a division is an army unit, but also a vote in Parliament, where a measure for one person or body is voted on.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament votes in a division on measures affecting particular persons or bodies, as opposed to public ones.

clue.text: Fancy Day was one

parts.note: Fancy Day is the heroine of Thomas Hardy's novel Under the Greenwood Tree, who teaches at the village school

explanation.surface: A remark about a fanciful day in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy Day' looks like a phrase about an imagined day, but it is a character's name in Hardy's Under the Greenwood Tree, where she is the village teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy's Fancy Day is the young teacher at the village school, a female teacher of pupils.

clue.text: Double the drive makes for double the earnings

definitions.meaning: a ship with two propellers has its drive doubled
screw is British slang for wages, so two of them is twice the pay

explanation.surface: A remark that working twice as hard doubles pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screw' is old British slang for a wage.
explanation.definitionFit: Two propellers drive the ship, and two wage packets read the same phrase as a pair of pay.

clue.text: Terrier a bear need make up to

indicators.note: to make up something is to compose it from parts, so these letters are put together afresh

explanation.surface: A bear must put on makeup to resemble a terrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make up' rearranges BEAR NEED; 'a' and 'to' link.
explanation.definitionFit: This Scottish breed of terrier takes its name from the city in north-east Scotland.

clue.text: Altogether a sanguine lot ?

parts.note: sanguine means cheerful but comes from the Latin for blood, so a sanguine lot is read as a group linked by blood

explanation.surface: A description of a wholly optimistic group of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sanguine' means hopeful in the surface; its root sense of blood gives family linked by birth.
explanation.definitionFit: Kin connected by birth or descent share blood, unlike in-laws who join by marriage.

clue.text: After work it reverts to silence, as is best

indicators.note: after work tells the solver the next pieces follow the work piece

parts.note: op is the abbreviation for opus, a work

indicators.note: reverts means the little word it is turned back to front

parts.note: mum means silent, as in keeping mum

explanation.surface: After a job is done, things go quiet, which is ideal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reverts' turns IT into TI; 'to' and 'as is' link.
explanation.definitionFit: The most favourable condition or amount is the ideal one.

clue.text: Russian girl turns to greet the devil

indicators.note: turns means the greeting and the devil together are read in reverse

parts.note: ah is an exclamation used in greeting
Satan is the devil

explanation.surface: A Russian girl turns round to welcome the devil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses AH SATAN to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A common Russian name for women, like Tolstoy's heroine in War and Peace.

clue.text: Precious lot of use a lever sounds to have been

definitions.note: the definition is a verb phrase standing for the past participle, the lot of something levered open

indicators.note: sounds means the word for precious is heard, while a different spelling is written

parts.note: something precious is prized

explanation.surface: A lever, a valuable piece of kit, sounds as if it was well used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lot of' and 'to have been' link: the fate of a thing someone used a lever on is to have been levered, which sounds like 'precious'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lid forced open with a crowbar has been levered, which is this word.

clue.text: It's up below the bridge

parts.note: the bridge is the bridge of the nose, and the word describes a nose whose tip turns up

explanation.surface: Something raised just under a river bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: The bridge here is the bridge of the nose; the answer is the French word for a turned-up nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A nose tilted upward at the tip is described with this French borrowing.

clue.text: Roared its head off in a row

indicators.note: its head off means the first letter of roared is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone shouted until hoarse during a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a row' reads as a quarrel, but means rowing a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Propelled by oars, as a boat moving with rowers is.

clue.text: Bacchic type trays

annotationWithheld.why: Bacchic type trays (5): the anagram of 'trays' has no indicator; 'type' belongs to the definition 'Bacchic type', so using it as the anagram signal would make it do two jobs

clue.text: Rice of the summer

parts.note: the American playwright Rice wrote The Adding Machine, and a summer is read as one who sums, an adding machine

explanation.surface: A grain harvested in the summer months.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summer' is read as one that sums: the playwright Elmer Rice wrote The Adding Machine (1923).
explanation.definitionFit: The American dramatist Rice, author of The Adding Machine, had this first name.

clue.text: Single blooms, said Perdita

parts.note: in The Winter's Tale Perdita speaks of pale spring flowers that die unmarried, so single means unwed

explanation.surface: A girl comments on flowers grown with single heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single' looks like a gardening term; it means unmarried, from Perdita's 'pale primroses, That die unmarried' in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Perdita describes these pale yellow spring flowers as dying unmarried, hence single blooms.

clue.text: Nineteenth century philanthropic body

parts.note: the American banker George Peabody was a famous philanthropist, and his surname is this word followed by body

explanation.surface: A charitable organisation of the 1800s.
explanation.walkthrough: George Peabody was a 19th-century philanthropist who funded housing in London; 'body' is the rest of his name, so the answer is what goes before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Peabody, the Victorian benefactor, has a surname made of this vegetable plus body.

clue.text: A bit of old Algeria

parts.note: the ancient Berber kingdom in North Africa covered much of what is now Algeria

explanation.surface: A small fragment of Algerian history.
explanation.definitionFit: This ancient North African kingdom, ruled by kings such as Jugurtha, lay largely within modern Algeria.

clue.text: Suitable country for cows, but not mountain sheep ?

definitions.text: Suitable country for cows, but not mountain sheep

parts.words: Suitable country for cows, but not mountain sheep
parts.note: cows low, so land for lowing beasts is the flat ground below, and mountain sheep want high ground

explanation.surface: Farming advice about which terrain suits cattle rather than hill sheep.
explanation.walkthrough: Cows low (moo), so low land suits them; mountain sheep need high ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat country near sea level suits grazing cattle, unlike hills or uplands.
